# Connect your project to GitHub {#sec-connect-github}

Now that you've created your project and have set up and authenticated your
computer with GitHub, you will now upload your project to GitHub. Before we do
that though, you'll need to do a few things. First, let's tell Git to ignore
some specific files, like the `.html` files as well as the `_files/` folders
that Quarto automatically creates when rendering your `.qmd` files. While in the
`AdvancedR3` project in RStudio, go to the Console and run this function to
ignore the auto-generated Quarto files.

```{r}
#| label: ignore-html-files
#| filename: "Console"
#| eval: false

usethis::use_git_ignore(c("*.html", "*_files"))
```

This will update the `.gitignore` file with these files to ignore. Next, you'll
need to commit your changes to Git, so that you can eventually push them to
GitHub. As mentioned in the [Setup Git](setup-git.qmd) (@sec-setup-git) section,
because we already covered Git in the introductory workshop, we won't go into it
in much detail in this workshop. However, during the workshop, you'll get plenty
of exposure and practice using Git. For these pre-workshop tasks, you can either
use the RStudio Git interface or use R functions in the Console.

**If you are familiar enough with using the RStudio Git interface**, then open
the Git interface with either the Git icon at the top near the menu bar or with
{{< var keybind.commit >}}. While in the interface, select all the current
changes by clicking the checkbox beside the files and stage them. Then write a
commit message in the text box on the right, something like
`Setting up the project`. Click the "Commit" button, and finally close the Git
interface.

**If you have never used the Git interface before**, you can instead copy and
paste these R functions to do the same thing. So paste these functions into the
Console and run them:

```{r}
#| label: add-to-git-history
#| filename: "Console"
#| eval: false

gert::git_add(".")
gert::git_commit("Setting up the project")
```

This will do the same thing as the Git interface, which is to save all the
changes to the Git history.

After adding the changes to the Git history, this should be the first commit for
everyone. You're now ready to connect your project to GitHub. In the Console,
run:

```{r}
#| label: use-github
#| filename: "Console"
#| eval: false

usethis::use_github()
```

::: callout-note
You may have to manually enter your username and password, even though you used
`gitcreds::gitcreds_set()`.

If you have troubles logging in, you may need to update Git.
:::

::: callout-tip
You might notice the word `origin` when referring to remotes. The word *origin*
is the default short name used to refer to the location of the remote (the
GitHub URL). You will probably see this word in many other places to refer to a
remote.
:::

The `usethis::use_github()` function will take your project and upload it to
GitHub. A bunch of text should pop up and it should open a browser with your
project on GitHub. You'll eventually need to copy and paste the URL for this new
GitHub repository into the survey at the end. You can always find your GitHub
repository by running `usethis::browse_github()` in the Console.

As you work on this project during the workshop, you'll be synchronising changes
regularly with it by "pushing" (uploading) and "pulling" (downloading). Using
Git and GitHub is one of the most effective ways to collaborate on a project.
Hundreds of companies and hundreds of thousands of workers use Git and services
like GitHub to work together on massive projects. The way collaboration works
would conceptually look like:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-local-collab-and-remote
%%| fig-cap: Schematic showing a local repository, GitHub's remote repository,
%%|   and a collaborator's repository.

graph TB;
    yours(Your local<br>repository) -->|Push| github(GitHub remote<br>repository)
    github -->|Pull| yours
    others(Collaborator's<br>local repository) -->|Push| github
    github -->|Pull| others
```

This approach to collaborating makes it much easier to contribute *directly*
(not through emails) to projects and to more easily help others out with issues.

You'll get more practice using GitHub during the workshop, and you'll have lots
of chances to ask questions about it.
